body_markdown:
The latest values in our price guide went live at the beginning of this month, and last week we discussed[bright spots](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/hagerty-price-guide/5-cars-gaining-value-in-a-split-market/) in the market, but also alluded to the fact that things are very divided at the moment. The collector car market is currently running at two distinct speeds: breakneck pace for modern supercars and notable slowing for older, established enthusiast vehicles. While no vehicle saw the rug pulled out from under it this past quarter, it is clear that willingness or ability to pay a premium for the average enthusiast vehicle is waning. From our latest update, here are a few of the standout vehicles that experienced a notable softening in value (as calculated across all conditions).


*Have questions about how we arrived at these changes? You can read more about the methodology behind the Hagerty Price Guide[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/how-the-hagerty-price-guide-is-made/) .*


## [1957–61 Jaguar XK 150](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=jaguar+xk+150)


Hagerty


**Average decrease:** -19%


The XK 150 was the last of Jaguar’s XK series of sports cars built through the 1940s and ’50s, and it represented a clear evolution from the[XK 120](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jaguar/xk_120/1953/1953-jaguar-xk_120-base?id=aCn1I000000CvHdSAK) and[XK 140](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jaguar/xk_140/1955/1955-jaguar-xk_140-base?id=aCn1I000000D1zhSAC) that came before it. The body was wider and more rounded, with a higher beltline, a one-piece curved windshield, and a roomier cabin that made it more comfortable for everyday use. It came as a Fixed-Head Coupe, a Drophead Coupe (convertible to us Americans), and an open Roadster.


Power came from Jaguar’s enduring XK twin-cam inline-six, which was available in several states of tune. The most desirable of these were the “S” models, with triple carburetors and up to 265 horsepower. Four-wheel disc brakes also arrived in the XK 150’s run, which was a major technical upgrade that put Jaguar well ahead of most of its rivals. It was both quicker and more refined than its predecessors, and it ended the XK era on a high note.


[Matt Fink](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mfinkhagerty-com/)


Those same qualities have made the XK 150 one of the more appealing buys among Jaguar’s postwar sports cars. It has the long-hood, wire-wheel look people want from a sporting ’50s British car, with a more usable cabin and better brakes than the earlier XKs. Parts support is good, and the club and specialist network is strong, which makes ownership easier than many other cars from the period. But the XK 150 is also a long-established model in the classic car hobby, and with big shifts in enthusiast attention to more modern performance cars, demand for cars like the XK softens.


There are some nuances in the XK 150’s softening this past quarter. The Drophead models remained little changed, while the Coupes bore the brunt of the decrease, with driver-quality (condition #3) examples of the sportier “S” versions dipping below the $50,000 mark. Still a chunk of change for most hobbyists, but a clear indication that the market is moving in a new direction.


Insurance quote data, which is a good indicator of ownership and interest, points to the vast majority of the XK 150’s fanbase being baby boomers. That cohort makes up 60% of quotes for XK 150s, while millennials and Gen-X combined only carry 25% of quotes. Does this mean sporty Jags are fading into obscurity? No, but it does put into focus the changes going on in the market at the moment.


## [2018, 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon/Demon 170](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=dodge+challenger+SRT+Demon)


Mecum


**Average decrease:** -18%


For 2018, Dodge built the Demon with one goal: Be the quickest, most extreme factory drag car, but still street legal. The recipe started with a supercharged 6.2-liter Hemi V-8 making 808 hp on pump gas and 840 on race fuel with a specialized ECU installed. The package helped this new king of all Challengers through the quarter-mile in the nine-second range straight from the showroom. Dodge also added a transbrake, a feature previously seen only on specially modified drag cars, as well as a long list of drag-strip hardware. A front passenger’s seat was not standard equipment; it was an available option for a single dollar.


Then, in 2023, Dodge took the Demon concept to its limit with the Demon 170. The blown Hemi engine now produced up to 1025 hp (when running E85 fuel). Billed as a sendoff for Dodge’s gas-powered V-8 muscle cars, it was built in limited numbers and sold out quickly, with many owners being 2018 Demon customers who chose to spec out their Demon 170 exactly like their 2018, even down to a matched VIN.


Stellantis


That backstory is a big part of why these cars have become such a hot commodity. Few modern cars have ever matched the Demon’s combination of outrageous performance while still being (barely) street legal. The production numbers are small as well. With the Challenger gone from the lineup and the V-8 muscle car era seemingly winding down, the Demon may very well be the high-water mark of the era, and the Demon 170 in particular has the added appeal of being the final chapter.


This recent change in value trajectory for the Demons has us very interested. When the 2018 model hit the market, the demand was such that they were instantly selling for over MSRP on the secondary market, and that trend held. Then the Demon 170 was announced, and Dodge captured that same energy with their “Last Call” lineup, cleverly marketing the end of the era. Now that the dust and demand have settled a bit, so have Demon prices.


A pristine, low- or no-mile Demon 170 has dropped from $164,000 on the top end (condition #1) to $134,000 in the past quarter. Because many viewed Demons as collectible from day one, there is no shortage of delivery-mile cars on the market and at auction, and they’re not bringing the same money they used to. And it’s not just the Demon that’s dropping—the[Hellcat](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=dodge+challenger+hellcat) dropped by 8%, too. As the hype for the high-spec Challenger settles down and with supply and demand reaching equilibrium, we may be shifting to a buyer’s market.


## [1960–63 Imperial](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1960+imperial)


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


**Average decrease:** -14%


Chrysler spun Imperial off as its own luxury brand in the mid-1950s, aiming to take on Cadillac and Lincoln, and the 1960–63 cars show just how much swagger it brought to the market. For 1960, Imperial remained a body on frame design as the rest of Chrysler moved to unibody, and under the hood sat a 413-cid V-8 backed by the pushbutton TorqueFlite automatic. Output was 340–350 hp.


The styling grew bolder every year, and the 1961 redesign brought the car’s most memorable feature: freestanding headlamps perched atop the bumpers in a nod to the classic cars of the 1930s. Upright rear fins and plush interiors were Imperial hallmarks, and the cars were available in Custom, Crown, and LeBaron trim.


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


Imperial as a brand disappeared after 1975, and again after a brief revival from 1981–83, so while vintage Imperials haven’t exactly been forgotten, they’ve long been overshadowed by the Cadillacs and Lincolns that dominated luxury sales in the era. That’s not changing, and Imperial prices are dropping.


There are a few factors at play here. The majority of insurance quotes on these types of vehicles come from an aging core demographic. Restoration costs are higher than ever, and with large ’50s American cars that wear tons of chrome and intricate trim, bills can be huge. This isn’t necessarily an Imperial-only problem; it just happens to be one of the cars demonstrating the challenges faced by ’50s domestics at the moment. These types of cars need to be sorted to sell, or at a low enough price point to make fixing palatable. But with excellent condition cars, specifically the Hardtop Coupes in the mid-$20,000 range, these stately Imperials can be had at a very attractive price for someone wanting a cruiser that makes a statement on a budget.


## [1947–55 Chevrolet Series 3100 Pickups](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/series_3100/1955/1955-chevrolet-series_3100-1!!2_ton?id=aCn1I000000DMKRSA4)


Paul Mehaffey


**Average decrease:** -9%


When Chevrolet rolled out its Advance Design trucks in mid-1947, it marked the first ground-up redesign of the brand’s pickups since before the war. The 3100, the half-ton model, was the one most buyers went for, and it brought big improvements to a segment that had been all work and little comfort. The cab was wider and roomier, with a bench seat that could actually fit three, and the optional Deluxe cab added rear corner windows and better trim. Under the hood sat Chevy’s dependable inline-six, which grew from 216 to 235 cubic inches in 1950 and delivered more power and torque.


The 3100 also saw steady improvements through its run, including a one-piece windshield in 1954 and the availability of the Hydramatic automatic beginning in 1953. It was a farm and jobsite truck first, but it was also an early step in pickups becoming everyday vehicles.


Hagerty Marketplace


Those same qualities explain why the 3100 has become such a popular collectible. These trucks are simple to work on, and parts support is outstanding. The styling, with its rounded fenders, bold grille, and honest proportions, has become the signature classic American pickup. They’re also easy to enjoy, whether in original configuration, lightly updated driver, or hot rod with a modern powertrain. Because Chevrolet built them in big numbers, there are plenty to choose from, making them an affordable entry into the classic truck world.


Trucks overall haven’t been as hot as they once were and have shifted from hot commodity to a[more rational market](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/old-trucks-are-the-smart-money-now/) , where smart enthusiasts can get in without breaking the bank. While popular entries like Blazers, Broncos, and Scouts are still expensive for their utilitarian nature, older pickups are where the deals are materializing. After the recent update, an Advance Design Chevrolet can be had for just above $20,000 for a clean example, putting these solidly in the “affordable” realm. While the average owner is trending on the older side per our quote data, trucks in general have a broad appeal, which may see a surge in activity among younger buyers for well-priced examples.


## [1990–95 Chevrolet Corvette ZR-1](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/1990/1990-chevrolet-corvette-zr~1?id=aCn1I000000CyvjSAC)


Chris Stark


**Average decrease:** -8%


When the ZR-1 arrived for 1990, it marked the first time in nearly two decades that Chevrolet’s sports car had a true performance halo above the rest of the lineup. The big news was under the hood: the LT5, a Lotus-designed, 5.7-liter, DOHC V-8 with 32 valves, assembled by Mercury Marine in Stillwater, Oklahoma. Output started at 375 horsepower and climbed to 405 for 1993, which was enough to push the C4 past 170 mph and into the conversation with Europe’s best. The ZR-1 also got a wider rear end with convex taillights and a price tag roughly double that of a standard Corvette.


Looking back, the ZR-1 wasn’t just a fast Corvette, but also a statement of intent. GM had spent years proving the Corvette could be a great sports car, and the ZR-1 proved it could be an uncompromising one, with a bespoke engine and a spot at the top of the range that the standard car could never claim. That idea lived on with the Z06 and ZR1 models that followed.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


The ZR-1 hasn’t escaped the cooling that has reached much of the established collector car market. Following a notable increase in value last year, the recent drop brings condition #3 (good) ZR-1 values to the lowest they’ve been in nearly five years. A #3 car can be had in the $25,000 range now, and we’ve even seen a few outliers of great cars selling for less in some cases.


What gives? Well, the ZR-1 isn’t exactly as simple to own as a standard C4 Corvette with its exotic engine, but that hardly seems to be a big detractor to the casual fan. It could simply be that despite all the technological leaps the ZR-1 made, the C5 is holding it back. That’s because for marginally less money, you can score a[C5 Z06](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2003/2003-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000CrvHSAS) , which is a better-performing car that enjoys much better parts support today. Either way, the ZR-1 represents a great buy for a car that’s faster than much more valuable stuff from the same era.
